title: Trump staffing changes post-midterms signal he's battle ready
description:
President Trump is making changes to his inner circle that signal how he may approach divided government.   

    
        
          Transcrip
body:
President Trump is making changes to his inner circle that signal how he may approach divided government.   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    ROB SCHMITZ, HOST:  President Trump says he's open to working with Democrats, but the staffing moves he's been making indicate otherwise. After a crushing defeat in the midterms for his party, the president is replacing his chief of staff, Susie Wiles, with hard-liner Stephen Miller. He has described the Democratic Party as a, quote, "domestic extremist organization." Joining us now to talk about this is White House correspondent Franco Ordoñez, who is traveling with the president in Palm Beach, Florida. Hey, Franco.FRANCO ORDOÑEZ, BYLINE: Hey, Rob.SCHMITZ: So I want to ask you more about Stephen Miller, but let's first turn to Susie Wiles. How big of a deal is her departure?ORDOÑEZ: Yeah. I mean, it's a very big deal, and it really is all wrapped together. Susie Wiles, you know, led Trump's campaign. She led his return to the White House. And she really is a historymaker, I mean, the first female White House chief of staff. And perhaps, more importantly, you know, she was really considered a stabilizing force in the administration. She brought discipline to a place, you know, that really has a lot of competing personalities.SCHMITZ: So what kind of White House do you expect under Stephen Miller?ORDOÑEZ: Well, Stephen Miller is one of the most uncompromising political ideologues pressing for Trump's agenda. He is the architect of some of Trump's most controversial policies, including border policies and the mass deportation raids that led to a significant level of political backlash. Miller is also very loyal, which is something Trump prizes. It means a lot to him, especially when he's under pressure like he is right now. And I'll just note - here is Miller talking this weekend at Mar-a-Lago.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)STEPHEN MILLER: We need to stand with the man who has stood with us and this country with every fiber of his being. It is the honor of my life to be President Trump's chief of staff. And I swear to you, and I pledge you, Mr. President, my absolute loyalty, my unwavering commitment and my total devotion to your success and the success of this country.ORDOÑEZ: And I'll just add, Rob, that Trump posted this video on his social media page.SCHMITZ: Wow, absolute loyalty - what does this mean for Trump working with Democrats?ORDOÑEZ: I do think it raises a lot of questions. As you noted at the top, Trump has expressed an openness to doing that. And here is a little bit of what he told us here in Florida when asked about what policies he could work with Democrats on.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP: I think a lot. I mean, I said before, immigrations one, tax cuts or maybe certain things having to do with taxes to make it more convenient and better, a lot of economic development initiatives we can do. I think we can do a lot of things together, actually. You know, a lot of them are about common sense also.ORDOÑEZ: So it really is a wait and see moment. I mean, Trump says he wants to work with Democrats, but the appointment of Miller and other comments, too, like posting a picture of a red MAGA hat saying Mr. Veto, suggesting, for example, the ultimate fighting chief to be the press secretary, it all just sends a different message. And just to put one more point on this, even some Republicans have spoken out about Miller's appointment, questioning whether Trump learned his lesson after such devastating midterm losses. You know, but as we've learned, Trump is going to do what Trump wants to do.SCHMITZ: Right. I mean, you mentioned Trump offering the press secretary job to Dana White, the chief executive of the Ultimate Fighting Championship. Is this for real?ORDOÑEZ: Yeah. I mean, I really do want to be careful with this because the president does have a tendency to kind of lure political opponents into controversy in order to draw attention to himself and then kind of make fun of the overreaction. The White House is not clarifying whether this is genuine. That said, Dana White did say, yesterday, that he was going to meet with the president on Monday to talk about this. And this president has done some surprising things. You know, whatever happens, I do think it speaks to a message being sent, and that is that the president is saying he has no plans on backing down, and he is preparing to fight moving forward.SCHMITZ: That is White House correspondent Franco Ordoñez. Franco, thank you.ORDOÑEZ: Thank you, Rob.

title: How will Democrats approach foreign policy after their midterm win?
description: NPR's Rob Schmitz speaks with Thomas Wright, senior fellow at the Brookings Institution, about his piece in Foreign Affairs titled The Fight fo
body:
NPR's Rob Schmitz speaks with Thomas Wright, senior fellow at the Brookings Institution, about his piece in Foreign Affairs titled The Fight for the Future of Democratic Foreign Policy.   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    ROB SCHMITZ, HOST:  Meanwhile, Democrats will have a majority in both chambers of Congress next year, and with the midterms behind them, they're looking to the 2028 presidential race. But there are differences within the Democratic Party on where U.S. foreign policy goes from here. Tom Wright is a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution and was a senior director for strategic planning at the National Security Council in the Biden administration. His latest article in Foreign Affairs is titled "The Fight For The Future Of Democratic Foreign Policy." Welcome.TOM WRIGHT: Thank you. It's good to be with you.SCHMITZ: So I've been an international correspondent for 16 years, but the last two may have been the busiest. The Trump administration threatened to take Greenland. It swooped into Venezuelan and snatched its authoritarian leader. It launched a trade war with the world's biggest economies, and it started a war with Iran. Looking ahead to 2028, what is the Democratic strategy on how to conduct foreign policy in the wake of this second term of President Trump?WRIGHT: Yeah, I think we're headed for a debate between different groups. Everyone agrees, I think, that Donald Trump has taken U.S. foreign policy in a destabilizing and dangerous direction. Everyone opposes, you know, the war in Iran and his attempt to take Greenland and the full-scale trade war. But there are, I think, substantive differences emerging on this sort of affirmative case that a future Democratic administration should make and whether or not they should build on what the Biden administration did or go in a more progressive direction. And I think those debates are very early, but I think that's what we can expect over the next 18 months of a primary campaign.SCHMITZ: So let's dig into these differences a little. The U.S. war with Iran and its impact on fuel prices were decisive issues in the midterms. An SSRS poll of voters showed that 63% of voters said the war in Iran was the wrong decision. We don't know how or when that conflict will resolve. How do you think Democrats might try to deal with the war if it is still an issue come January?WRIGHT: Everyone, whether their centrists or progressive, you know, opposed the war that began on February 28 of this year. But as we get into a new Congress, there will probably be votes on funding the rest of the military. Basically, all of the potential candidates believe that this was the wrong decision, and they've criticized it from the beginning, and they want to bring it to an end. I think they also recognize that there's no good options at this point, that we're in a situation of Donald Trump's making where there isn't really a good deal on the table, and there certainly aren't good military options. So any end is likely to be messy and suboptimal.SCHMITZ: Well, elsewhere in the Middle East, you know, one consistent sticking point within the Democratic Party is, of course, Israel. We could see the end of Benjamin Netanyahu's leadership as prime minister soon. Explain the big division among Democrats on Israel.WRIGHT: That's definitely, I think, the most contentious issue. The progressives have tended to go further, and they've argued for more sort of sustained pressure on Israel. So I think there's been a shift on both sides, so to speak, but there will still be a debate about how far that change should go.SCHMITZ: There is also division among Democrats on how to handle China. Are Democrats more likely to deal with China as a threat or as a potential partner?WRIGHT: That's a big debate. I think the Biden administration treated China as a competitor...SCHMITZ: Right.WRIGHT: ...And had a strategy of, you know, managed competition. The Trump administration has generally stepped back from strategic competition. Some progressives have actually welcomed the Trump administration's policy, particularly in the second year, as creating real breathing room, as they call it, in U.S.-China relations. And I think Democrats are set up for a big debate about whether or not to go back to some version of managed competition.SCHMITZ: We've been talking about a lot of divisions within the Democratic Party on foreign policy. I want to move here to Russia and its war with Ukraine. Is this an area where Democrats might find more common ground?WRIGHT: Yeah, Europe really hasn't figured all that much, and Russia-Ukraine hasn't figured all that much in the internal debates over the last couple of years. There's really very few, if any, on the progressive side who, you know, are sympathetic to Putin or Russia. There's broad agreement that Putin is a dangerous and destabilizing influence in world affairs, that the U.S. can't really cooperate or work with Russia. I think the new Congress is likely to appropriate more funding for Ukraine. My expectation would be that progressives would support that. So - but it is, I think, one of those issues that has not really arisen yet in the internal debate, which suggests to me that, basically, all sides are generally comfortable with some policy of support for Ukraine.SCHMITZ: The lesson of the midterms is that American voters turned out for mostly domestic issues. To what extent will foreign policy be a priority for Democrats?WRIGHT: Yeah, I think foreign policy actually featured more in this midterm election maybe than in any midterm election that I can think of since just after 9/11 because it was - obviously, the Iran war and its effect on affordability was a major concern, particularly in red states, but also, I think tariffs had a huge impact in Ohio and Kansas.SCHMITZ: I mean, these are domestic issues with foreign causes, right?WRIGHT: Right. But they are - they're foreign policy issues decisions that I think had a domestic impact...SCHMITZ: Right.WRIGHT: ...In terms of the consequences. So, you know, tariffs is a trade, you know, policy decision. The war in Iran clearly was a foreign policy decision. But they directly impacted on voters in the United States. And I think that, you know, may still be the case in 2028, in that if Donald Trump continues to wage war in Iran, which I think it's quite possible - even if he would like to get out, Iran may not facilitate that on terms that will be acceptable to him - if he continues to push on tariffs and if there are new, you know, decisions and actions that have real repercussions, I think that will impact on voters pretty directly.And then I think there are very large questions to do with China, Russia and others that reflect, you know, the fact that the international situation today is probably one of the most difficult and fraught in many decades. And so the stakes are quite high. And so I think there will be a pretty fundamental choice presented to the voters, both in the primary campaign and then in the general election, and that's right and proper and as it should be.SCHMITZ: That is Tom Wright. He's a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution. Thanks.WRIGHT: Thank you.(SOUNDBITE OF MARISA ANDERSON'S "HESITATION THEME AND VARIATION BLUES")

title: Congress is coming back to Washington. Here's what to expect
description:
Congress is coming back to Washington. Here's what to expect
    
        
                Download
body:
Congress is coming back to Washington. Here's what to expect
    
        
                Download
                
                
                    
                        
                            
                            Embed
                        
                        
                            <iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/nx-s1-6030633/nx-s1-9996853" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player">
                        
                    
                
        
    



      
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Lawmakers are returning to Washington this week to finish up work before Democrats take control of the House and Senate in January.
                
                    Zayrha Rodriguez/NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Zayrha Rodriguez/NPR
    

   
   It is the final hoorah for the 119th Congress. Republicans have just weeks left in control of the House of Republicans and the Senate. The main thing on the agenda: keeping the federal government open. Funding is set to run out on December 11, when a stop-gap measure passed about a month ahead of the midterms expires.   Any funding extension is all but certain to be done through another short-term bill, known as a continuing resolution. The typical government funding process — 12 carefully negotiated appropriations bills — would take time and political will that lawmakers currently lack.   
   Congress will also need to find a path forward on the National Defense Authorization Act, long considered a must-pass annual military funding package. This year, the bill is quagmired in the unforgiving politics of the Iran war. The conflict is opposed by a majority of Americans — something President Trump has acknowledged was a key force in driving his party out of power.   The House is also likely to vote on an impeachment effort targeting Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth. Introduced by Republican Thomas Massie of Kentucky, a key figure in forcing the administration's release of the Epstein files, the impeachment measure lists a number of charges, including that the administration failed to properly consult Congress on the military campaign.   
   Democrats are unlikely to be in a compromising mood on legislation, just weeks away from taking control of both chambers. That means continued work on big-ticket items like the Protect College Sports Act, meant to introduce new regulations around college athlete compensation, and a bipartisan energy permitting overhaul will likely wait until the new term.   With slim majorities in both chambers, they could also have to contend with some attendance problems after a demoralizing performance in last week's midterm elections. That further complicates passing legislation through chambers already governed by the thinnest of majorities.   
   Mike Ricci, a Republican strategist with the group Seven Letter and aide to former Speakers of the House John Boehner and Paul Ryan, told NPR that a number of forces could help draw reluctant lame duck legislators back to Washington, including winding down their offices, finding new work and attending the White House Christmas party.

title: Democrats won big. Can they lower your grocery bill?
description: A supporter holds a sign during a campai
body:
A supporter holds a sign during a campaign rally for Democratic Senate candidate Dr. Annie Andrews in Myrtle Beach, S.C., on Nov. 1. Andrews defeated her Republican opponent, Sen. Darline Graham.
                
                    Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images
    

   
   It's been a feature of campaign ads and stump speeches for months: grocery prices are out of control.   
   Affordability concerns, including high food costs, were top of mind for voters heading into the midterms, as the Trump administration's tariffs and the war in Iran continued to drive up prices. That economic strain helped Democrats win control of both houses of Congress on Tuesday.   House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries said the incoming majority would make tackling high prices a priority come January. "It was a tremendous victory for the American people and a strong rebuke of MAGA extremism, which has made life more expensive for everyday Americans despite their promises to lower the high cost of living on day one," he told NPR on Friday.   
   The question is how Democrats will do that with President Trump still in the Oval Office, willing to wield his veto pen. Senate Democrats won't have a filibuster-proof majority, and Trump may have little appetite to roll back his signature tariffs or reverse course on the Iran war, two of the main causes of high food prices.   Lael Brainard, who leads a public policy group called The Kitchen Table Project, said Americans are nevertheless expecting relief from Washington — and quickly.   "They are feeling like they are getting squeezed by high prices that don't need to be that high," she said.   What Democrats plan to do to lower food prices   Despite the political hurdles, Democrats said they intend to move ahead with plans to cut grocery bills, including by rolling back Trump's tariffs. Those tariffs have not only raised the cost of certain foods and drinks imported to the U.S., but also created other pressures on the food industry by making it more expensive to import things like machine parts and packaging.   
   The Iran war has led to a surge in energy prices, which has made it more expensive to transport just about everything. Fertilizer costs also grew when the closure of the Strait of Hormuz cut off a significant portion of the global fertilizer trade.   But getting Trump to backtrack on tariffs or the Iran war — or his immigration crackdown, which has led to labor shortages on U.S. farms — could prove tricky for Democrats.   "I think the president would certainly want to find ways to reduce the cost of groceries. Democrats [also] see that in their interest," said Lehigh University political science professor Chris Borick. "The mechanisms, the tools, the levers that would be most readily available to do that — there's quite a bit of distance between the president and Democrats that'll be taking over both the House and the Senate."   
   Several incoming Democratic senators also floated other proposals during their campaigns that aim to make groceries more affordable.   James Talarico of Texas said he would push back against "attacks" on the federal food assistance programs WIC and SNAP, the latter of which is undergoing a major overhaul by the Trump administration and has seen a precipitous drop in participation since last summer. Kansas' Adam Hamilton announced his support for a national ban on "dynamic pricing" in grocery stores. And multiple candidates, including Roy Cooper of North Carolina, vowed to block food industry mergers they say would raise consumer prices.   Democratic governors take a piece of the affordability pie   Beyond the blue wave in Congress, Democrats also made gains in state capitals across the U.S. on Tuesday. At least 28 states will have Democratic governors beginning next year, and ten state legislative chambers flipped to Democrats, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures.   
   Incoming state governors have floated their own ideas for how to give residents relief in the grocery aisle.   Keisha Lance Bottoms proposed allowing municipalities in Georgia to suspend or fully eliminate their local sales tax on groceries, baby formula, diapers and more. Gina Hinojosa, the governor-elect of Texas, promised to outlaw "predatory surveillance pricing" and price gouging in grocery stores. In New Mexico, Deb Haaland said the state would explore a policy similar to one in Albuquerque that temporarily waives permitting fees for markets that sell healthy and affordable food in so-called "food deserts," the Albuquerque Journal reported.   However state and federal officials decide to go about lowering prices, Americans say they want to see cheaper groceries soon. According to a poll released by the Kitchen Table Project and Global Strategy Group in September, nearly half of respondents said their most important goal was seeing their grocery bills lowered within six months.

title: Supreme Court weighs effort to shield federal law enforcement as ICE complaints rise
description: The Supreme Court is seen on Oct. 1 in W
body:
The Supreme Court is seen on Oct. 1 in Washington, D.C.
                
                    J. Scott Applewhite/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        J. Scott Applewhite/AP
    

   
   Five years ago, a gang riot broke out inside a federal prison in Hawaii.   Kekai Watanabe was beaten with a makeshift weapon known as a "lock in a sock."   When he complained about serious back pain, a nurse told him to "stop being a cry baby."   Seven months later, doctors diagnosed Watanabe with a fractured tail bone, and he sued the nurse for violating his Eighth Amendment right against cruel and unusual punishment.   
   On Monday, the Supreme Court will hear his case, which could determine whether federal law enforcement officers can be held to account when they violate constitutional rights. The claim by Watanabe, now 40, echoes far beyond the walls of prison — and into American streets where immigration officers have been accused of beating and running over migrants.   "What's at stake here is whether, basically, we as a country are going to hold federal law enforcement officers accountable when they violate clearly established constitutional rights," said Georgetown law professor Steve Vladeck, who filed a "friend of the court" brief in the case. "I mean, it really is, I think, that stark."   
   It's already difficult for these claims to proceed, because the court requires people to show the facts in their cases are identical to precedent. In the federal prisons, the landmark case dates to 1980. The prisoner in that lawsuit died from untreated asthma. The nurse's lawyers say Watanabe, the inmate from Hawaii, survived the gang attack in 2021, so his case is different enough that it should be dismissed.   
   Mary Hampton Mason worked at the Justice Department for nearly 35 years, in an office that evaluated these kinds of legal claims. Mason said rogue officers are rare, and problems are typically systemic.   "It's a result of agency culture, it's a result of training, it's a result of all sorts of things, but these failures are really institutional," Mason said.   The Supreme Court created a right to sue federal officers for wrongdoing in a 1971 case known as Bivens. But Mason said that precedent has been hollowed out for years, and the court should finally overrule it because it gives plaintiffs false hope.   "In fact in the last 20 years, I'm only aware of one Bivens case that has resulted in a judgment for the plaintiffs that … didn't get reversed on appeal, and that's in thousands and thousands and thousands of cases filed," she said.   
   But supporters of the prisoner say that number doesn't account for settlements or how these lawsuits can deter other bad behavior. If individual federal officers and agents can be on the hook financially, the argument goes, they could think twice before breaking the law.   "That's why damages are so important," said Gregory Cui, an attorney at the MacArthur Justice Center, a civil rights legal organization. "Because they're a way to try to fix things, to give a person the means to pay for medical care or rebuild their life."   In a "friend of the court" brief, Cui reported that the grievance process for people inside federal prison almost never works for inmates, who succeed just 1% of the time in changing things such as access to medical care or better conditions behind bars.   
   Cui and other legal experts said the Supreme Court agreed to hear this case at a time when abuses by federal immigration agents and others are in the spotlight. Now, they said, is the wrong time for the court to eliminate one of the few avenues of accountability for those errant officers.   "A world with no Bivens is a world in which federal law enforcement officers would enjoy absolute immunity, where no matter how egregious their conduct is, no one can hold them liable," said Vladeck, of Georgetown Law Center. "As alarming a prospect as that may have been five years ago, it should be an especially terrifying one today, and it ought to be one that even this Supreme Court is worried about endorsing."   Both sides agree Congress has the power to weigh in and give people whose rights have been violated by federal officers a clear way to sue. But so far lawmakers have not advanced legislation to hold those people to account.

title: No clear winner in New Zealand election, as leaders prepare for weeks of talks
description: New Zealand Prime Minister and National
body:
New Zealand Prime Minister and National Party leader, Christopher Luxon addresses party faithful in Auckland, New Zealand, Saturday, Nov.7, 2026.
                
                    Alex Robertson/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Alex Robertson/AP
    

   
   WELLINGTON, New Zealand — New Zealanders will wait for weeks to discover who will lead the country after Saturday's election failed to deliver a decisive win for the right or the left, leaving fraught negotiations for a wafer-thin governing majority the only apparent path to victory for either side.   The tightest vote in years delivered a stinging rebuke to the major parties which have long dominated New Zealand politics, Christopher Luxon's center-right National party and center-left Labour led by Chris Hipkins, as voters threw more support behind minor parties on the ideological flanks than before. On Saturday's numbers, minor parties would enter negotiations for a governing deal with leverage to extract deeper policy concessions from a weakened National or Labour.   
   The near-deadlock was partly produced because voters, apparently weary of New Zealand's economic woes and apathetic about both Luxon and Hipkins, chose to propel a new entrant group to Parliament for the first time in years. Opportunity, led by 38-year-old business consultant and political newcomer Qiulae Wong, is unaligned with either bloc and Wong has said she could work with either side to form a government.   Wong's pledges of evidence-based centrism and an end to partisan bickering had on Saturday's results secured seven seats for Opportunity — enough to frustrate both left and right in a simple path to power. It was a staggering ascension for a party that made three failed attempts at Parliament before Wong became leader less than a year ago.   The conservative bloc has a simpler route to victory, but results could change   Other winners were harder to identify and on Sunday, "who won the election 2026" was the top trending Google search in New Zealand. So unclear was the result that parties won't begin negotiations to form a government until final tallies are released on Nov. 27, confirming the exact number of seats they've won.   With 2.8 million ballots counted on election night, the conservative incumbent government led by Luxon's National party appeared close to the slimmest possible return to power — by just one seat. However, Luxon didn't claim victory, instead striking a note of cautious optimism that he could negotiate a second term in power.   
   Speaking to reporters Sunday, Luxon blamed public dissatisfaction on global shocks which have buffeted New Zealand's trade-based economy, noting that other incumbent governments worldwide have faced voters' rancor over living costs.   Yet his opponent Hipkins, who was turfed from office in 2023 largely over discontent about the same economic issues, didn't appear to benefit on Saturday. The left-wing bloc appeared to fall short of a majority but was still hopeful it could triumph — though that seemed a more remote prospect.   Electoral officials were due on Sunday to begin counting nearly 400,000 so-called special votes, including from New Zealanders who live abroad, a process expected to take three weeks.   Those ballots have historically granted an additional seat or two in Parliament to left-wing parties, which could snatch the current razor-thin majority from the right, although such an outcome would likely leave the left struggling to form a majority too. If a government can't be formed, New Zealand could face a fresh vote.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Labour Party leader Chris Hipkins addresses party faithful in Upper Hutt, New Zealand, Saturday, Nov. 7, 2026.
                
                    Mark Tantrum/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Mark Tantrum/AP
    

   
   Incumbent Luxon urges people to 'calm down' and enjoy a break from politics   "I think everyone's over politics so let's all have a bit of a break for the next three weeks," Luxon told reporters on Sunday. He will lead a caretaker government until an outcome is reached.   Luxon suggested that National had a viable path to power and boasted that it had secured more seats in Parliament than any other group. However, Saturday night was bleak for his party.   Several of National's most senior lawmakers would exit politics on results so far, including the ministers of finance and defense, the speaker of parliament, and the attorney general. With the party's traditional governing partners winning increased support, Luxon faces a more strident list of policy demands to secure their backing.   Libertarian ACT won 13 seats and populist New Zealand First won 12. Both are led by canny veteran politicians, and detractors of Luxon, a former business executive who entered politics in 2020, said his dealings with them in the three years since he took office had highlighted his political inexperience.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                The Opportunity Party leader Qiulae Wong poses for a portrait outside Parliament in Wellington, New Zealand, Friday, Oct. 30, 2026.
                
                    Charlotte Graham-McLay/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Charlotte Graham-McLay/AP
    

   
   The vote was a slap for both major parties   New Zealanders don't vote for prime ministers. Instead they cast two votes, one for their preferred party and another for the candidate they want as their local representative.   
   The country has one house of Parliament and no states, so the central government holds ultimate sway over New Zealand's direction. Governments in the South Pacific nation of 5.6 million people are elected every three years.   National won just 29.21% of the preferred party vote as of Sunday, a collapse of its previous result, and secured its 42 seats entirely by winning local constituency races. Luxon, who unusually faced two separateconfidence votes among his own lawmakers this year, further slumped in popularity as leader close to election day.   However, Labour also won just 29.36% of the party vote, a result that appeared to suggest a second election defeat for career politician Hipkins. Despite winning about the same party vote percentage as National, Labour has secured only 36 seats on numbers so far because they won fewer local races.   Minor parties on the left saw bolstered support. The environmentally-focused Greens won 16 seats and Indigenous rights group Te Pāti Māori secured five.   The total number of seats in New Zealand's Parliament changes due to quirks in how seat allocations are calculated. There would currently be 131 lawmakers elected, with 66 seats required for a majority.   Luxon's conservative bloc would currently hold 67, a razor-thin margin likely to discomfit a leader managing a three-way government with two emboldened minor parties. However, the left bloc held only 57 seats before the historically left-leaning special votes were counted.   Even if the final tally boosted the left bloc's seats slightly, Hipkins would apparently need support from newcomer Wong to govern.   Before the election, Luxon repeatedly ruled out negotiating with Wong. He sidestepped questions on Sunday about whether his vanishingly slim lead had changed his mind.

schema.headline: No clear winner in New Zealand election, as leaders prepare for weeks of talks

title: NPR's Moscow and Beijing correspondents discuss the reaction to U.S. elections abroad
description: The results of the U.S. midterms were closely followed overseas. NPR correspondents in Moscow and Beijing discuss how the elections are seen in
body:
The results of the U.S. midterms were closely followed overseas. NPR correspondents in Moscow and Beijing discuss how the elections are seen in the countries they cover.   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    AYESHA RASCOE, HOST:  Results of the U.S. midterms also created ripples around the world. To discuss the global impact of the election, we're joined now by NPR correspondents Charles Maynes in Moscow and Jennifer Pak in Beijing. Good morning to both of you.CHARLES MAYNES, BYLINE: Morning.JENNIFER PAK, BYLINE: Good morning.RASCOE: Charles, if we can start with you, how do you think President Putin will view the midterms?MAYNES: Well, President Putin hasn't spoken directly about the results, but the wider Kremlin approach has been quite transparent, which is to continue actively engaging President Trump. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov this week said Russia is sincerely counting on Trump to continue peace efforts in Ukraine and suggested those efforts had already made some progress, pointing to, for example, Melania Trump's humanitarian work. Also U.S.-led trilateral talks set to take place in Abu Dhabi next week. You know, contrast that with a senior Russian diplomat, the deputy foreign minister, Sergei Ryabkov, who said Moscow has long viewed Democrats as holding intensely negative views of Russia, so it's obvious who they'd rather deal with.RASCOE: And yet, though, that window of opportunity for dealing with Trump is closing.MAYNES: True. And there's broad acknowledgment that Trump will face more scrutiny from Democrats, including over his dealings with Russia when it comes to Ukraine. You know, at the heart of Trump's recent negotiations with Russia has been this idea that cutting deals with Moscow by offering sanctions relief, for example, that that can unlock Russian concessions over Ukraine, whether that's a good bet or not - and the administration would argue it is working - the midterm results, ironically, may open Russia up to negotiations, simply because Moscow may want to cut a more favorable deal with Trump before this new Congress is seated in January. But, of course, the clock's ticking.RASCOE: And, Jennifer, how is Beijing reacting?PAK: Well, officially, China has been quite measured because, like President Putin, Chinese leader Xi Jinping is not going anywhere. So the big question, of course, is is any deal really going to stick with Trump, given that President Xi is really going to be looking for a fourth term next year? He's expected to. So given that being tougher on China is now a bipartisan issue, that question is up in the air.The Chinese foreign ministry have said it's going to be business as usual, that China is willing to work with the U.S. on upholding what Trump and Xi had agreed upon in the earlier two summits this year, which is called the constructive strategic stability. It's quite a mouthful. But essentially, what it means is the two countries have acknowledged they're going to continue to compete, but that there should be some predictability or stability in the relationship.RASCOE: Charles, we've talked about Russia, but I want to turn to Ukraine. How are the results seen there?MAYNES: Yeah. You know, Ukraine is really the flip side of what we were talking about earlier. They're counting the days until this new Democratic-controlled Congress arrives because these incoming congressmen are seen as more sympathetic to Ukraine. It's a point made by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in an interview with Jake Tapper on CNN.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)PRESIDENT VOLODYMYR ZELENSKYY: They don't try to balance between us and Russia. They don't afraid to say that Russia is aggressor. They don't want to give our land to Putin. And I think that based on such things, of course, we count on even more support.MAYNES: You know, that said, Zelenskyy is clearly being careful not to antagonize Trump outright, aware, of course, that the president could make life very difficult for Ukrainians, even with the Democrats controlling Congress.RASCOE: President Trump and President Xi are expected to meet later this month in China. What's likely to be on the agenda?PAK: Well, we don't know yet, but this is essentially a trust-building exercise because, despite the pleasantries that have been exchanged between Trump and Xi and the warmth, the U.S. administration in between these summits have continually added more Chinese firms and individuals on blacklists. They've also banned, like, Chinese humanoids, drones from being imported into the U.S., while China, according to the U.S., continues to restrict the flow of rare earth to the U.S. and hasn't really followed through on his purchases of U.S. agricultural goods. So following through on the promises made in the last two summits is essentially going to be the goal.We have heard they've made progress on lowering tariffs on $60 billion worth of goods flowing between the two countries. They've identified which items that are non-sensitive, and that might be easier to push through because of the cost of living became a key issue in the midterms. The areas that are much harder to negotiate on are, for example, Chinese investments in the U.S., the American stance on Taiwan and also guardrails on AI. But the purpose, according to Chinese analysts I've spoken to, of these summits is to build mutual trust because there is just so little right now between the U.S. and China.RASCOE: And, Charles, the two leaders could be joined for the talks by President Putin. If that were to happen, how significant would that be?MAYNES: Well, it could be hugely significant, at least when it comes to Ukraine. A few days ago, Trump held a meeting at the White House with the Kremlin's envoy, a man by the name of Kirill Dmitriev, after which Trump said the U.S. and Russia were closing in on a peace deal for Ukraine that could also impact all of Europe. Let's listen to Trump.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP: It's going to be a big, beautiful agreement, and everyone's going to be thrilled.MAYNES: Now, Trump has repeatedly overstated his abilities to end this war. But the idea that he and Putin, or perhaps with input from Xi, could negotiate some grand superpower bargain while cutting Ukraine and Europe out of the loop is a fear that's dogged Trump's peace efforts since he returned to office. I think the catch here is that it's even harder now to imagine Ukraine or, for that matter, Europe, accepting those terms, given the midterm results and what's left of Trump's time in office.RASCOE: That's NPR correspondents Charles Maynes in Moscow and Jennifer Pak in Beijing. Thank you so much for joining us.MAYNES: Thank you.RASCOE: You're welcome.(SOUNDBITE OF PURE X'S "YOU'RE IN IT NOW")
